\section[el desfase horario]{el desfase horario — jet lag; the time difference}

\label{lesson:ES-C655-desfase-horario}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the crew, then the Spanish for the flight attendant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el desfase horario}
\textbf{el desfase horario} — \textquotedblleft{}jet lag; the time difference\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Con el desfase horario no duermo bien.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{With jet lag I do not sleep well.}
\end{quote}

Many people also say \emph{el jet lag}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desfase} is built on \emph{fase} \textquotedblleft{}phase\textquotedblright{}, from Greek \emph{phásis} \textquotedblleft{}appearance\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); \emph{horario} is built on \emph{hora} \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{hōra}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el desfase horario}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el desfase horario}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el desfase horario}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the crew, then the Spanish for the flight attendant, then say \emph{el desfase horario} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el desfase horario mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Jet lag; the time difference\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la turbulencia]{la turbulencia — the turbulence}

\label{lesson:ES-C655-turbulencia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the flight attendant, then the Spanish for jet lag.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la turbulencia}
\textbf{la turbulencia} — \textquotedblleft{}the turbulence\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hay turbulencias, abróchense el cinturón.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is turbulence, fasten your seat belts.}
\end{quote}

Often plural on a plane: \emph{hay turbulencias}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{turbulencia} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{turbulentia} (EtymDB), from \emph{turbulentus} \textquotedblleft{}restless, stormy\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{turba} \textquotedblleft{}uproar, crowd\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la turbulencia}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la turbulencia}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la turbulencia}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the flight attendant, then the Spanish for jet lag, then say \emph{la turbulencia} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la turbulencia mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The turbulence\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el mareo]{el mareo — travel sickness; dizziness}

\label{lesson:ES-C655-mareo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for jet lag, then the Spanish for the turbulence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el mareo}
\textbf{el mareo} — \textquotedblleft{}travel sickness; dizziness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Estas pastillas son para el mareo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{These pills are for travel sickness.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{marear}, which comes from \emph{mar}: the first \emph{mareo} was at sea.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mareo} is built on \emph{marear} \textquotedblleft{}to make seasick\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which comes from \emph{mar} \textquotedblleft{}sea\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{mare}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el mareo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el mareo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el mareo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for jet lag, then the Spanish for the turbulence, then say \emph{el mareo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el mareo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Travel sickness; dizziness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[marearse]{marearse — to feel sick (in a vehicle), to get dizzy}

\label{lesson:ES-C655-marearse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the turbulence, then the Spanish for travel sickness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: marearse}
\textbf{marearse} — \textquotedblleft{}to feel sick (in a vehicle), to get dizzy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me mareo si leo en el coche.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I feel sick if I read in the car.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Estar mareado} — to feel sick or dizzy.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{marearse} is built on \emph{mar} \textquotedblleft{}sea\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{mare} (EtymDB); it first meant to be seasick.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{marearse}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{marearse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{marearse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the turbulence, then the Spanish for travel sickness, then say \emph{marearse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does marearse mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To feel sick (in a vehicle), to get dizzy\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el chaleco]{el chaleco — the waistcoat, the vest}

\label{lesson:ES-C655-chaleco}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for travel sickness, then the Spanish for to feel sick.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el chaleco}
\textbf{el chaleco} — \textquotedblleft{}the waistcoat, the vest\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El chaleco salvavidas está debajo del asiento.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The life jacket is under the seat.}
\end{quote}

\emph{El chaleco salvavidas} — the life jacket.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{chaleco} is usually traced to Turkish \emph{yelek} \textquotedblleft{}waistcoat\textquotedblright{}, a word that reached Spanish through Arabic.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for travel sickness, then the Spanish for to feel sick, then say \emph{el chaleco} again
